\subsection*{Randomized --- Reductions: Results}

\begin{definition}[Randomized recognition with error bound]
\lean{Randomized.InBPPAt}
\statementsource{Vad12}{pdf-bf2ce5422088-p023-b001}
\statementsource{arora-barak-ch07-randomized-computation}{pdf-26d95080dbde-p003-b004}
\label{Randomized.InBPPAt}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.boolVerifier, Randomized.polyLen, Randomized.randProb}
A language $L$ belongs to the class at parameter $p$ if there are a randomized verifier
$M$ and natural numbers $a,k$ such that the verifier is efficient according to $E$, and
for every input $x$, its probability of outputting true is at least $p$ when $x\in L$,
while its probability of outputting false is at least $p$ when $x\notin L$. In both
cases the verifier uses randomness of length $a+k|x|$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Monotonicity of randomized verification]
\lean{Randomized.InBPPAt.mono}
\label{Randomized.InBPPAt.mono}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.InBPPAt}
\difficulty{4}
Let $E$ be a verifier model, let $L$ be a language of bit strings, and let
$p',p\in\mathbb{Q}$ satisfy $p'\le p$. If $L$ has an $E$-efficient randomized verifier
with polynomially bounded randomness whose acceptance probability on members and
rejection probability on nonmembers are each at least $p$, then it has such a verifier
with both probabilities at least $p'$.
\end{theorem}

  {Randomized.InBPPAt}
  {context}
  {arora-barak-ch07-randomized-computation}
  {pdf-26d95080dbde-p002-b003,
    pdf-26d95080dbde-p003-b004}
For every verifier model $E$ and every language $L$ of bit strings, $L$ is in BPP
relative to $E$ if and only if it has a polynomial-time randomized verifier whose
probability of outputting the correct membership bit is at least $2/3$ on every input.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Majority amplification of success probability]
\lean{Randomized.InBPPAt.amplify}
\label{Randomized.InBPPAt.amplify}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.ClosedUnderMajority, Randomized.InBPPAt, Randomized.blockCount, Randomized.blockCount_add_not, Randomized.majorityVerifier, Randomized.polyLen, Randomized.randProb, Randomized.randProb_bool_false, Randomized.randProb_congr, Randomized.randProb_mono, Randomized.randProb_not, Randomized.randProb_tail_le}
\difficulty{6}
Let $E$ be a verifier model closed under majority amplification, let $K\in\mathbb{N}$,
and let $\varepsilon,\eta\in\mathbb{Q}$ satisfy $0\le\varepsilon$ and
$2(1-4\varepsilon^2)^{\lfloor K/2\rfloor}\le\eta$. If a language $L$ is decidable using
$E$ with success probability at least $1/2+\varepsilon$ on every input, then it is
decidable using $E$ with success probability at least $1-\eta$ on every input.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Improved bounded-error success probability]
\lean{Randomized.InBPP.inBPPAt_23_24}
\label{Randomized.InBPP.inBPPAt_23_24}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.ClosedUnderMajority, Randomized.InBPP, Randomized.InBPPAt, Randomized.amplify_concrete, Randomized.polyLen}
\difficulty{4}
Let $E$ be a verifier model closed under majority amplification. If a language $L$ is
decidable using $E$ with success probability at least $2/3$ on every input, then it is
decidable using $E$ with success probability at least $23/24$ on every input.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Amplifying a 5/8 success probability]
\lean{Randomized.InBPPAt.inBPP_of_5_8}
\label{Randomized.InBPPAt.inBPP_of_5_8}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.ClosedUnderMajority, Randomized.InBPP, Randomized.InBPPAt, Randomized.InBPPAt.amplify, Randomized.InBPPAt.mono}
\difficulty{3}
Let $E$ be a verifier model whose efficient verifiers are closed under majority
repetition, and let $L$ be a language of bit strings. If some efficient randomized
verifier uses a number of random bits bounded by a polynomial in the input length and
accepts members of $L$, and rejects nonmembers, each with probability at least $5/8$,
then $L$ has such a verifier with both probabilities at least $2/3$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Randomized many-one reducibility]
\lean{Randomized.RandReducible}
\statementsource{arora-barak-ch07-randomized-computation}{pdf-26d95080dbde-p015-b002}
\label{Randomized.RandReducible}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.PolyTimeComputable, Randomized.polyLen, Randomized.randProb, Turing.pairEncode}
A language $B$ is randomized reducible to a language $C$ if there is a polynomial-time
computable function $f$ and natural numbers $a,k$ such that, for every input $x$, with
probability at least $2/3$ over a random string $r$ of length $a+k|x|$, membership of
the paired encoding of $x$ and $r$ in $C$ is equivalent to membership of $x$ in $B$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Polynomial reductions preserve randomized reducibility]
\lean{Randomized.RandReducible.of_polyTimeReducible}
\label{Randomized.RandReducible.of_polyTimeReducible}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.PolyTimeComputable.comp, Complexity.pairFstD, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_pairFstD, Randomized.randProb_congr, Randomized.randProb_true}
\difficulty{3}
Let $B$ and $C$ be languages of binary strings. If $B$ is polynomial-time many-one
reducible to $C$, then $B$ is randomized-reducible to $C$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Composition of polynomial and randomized reductions]
\lean{Randomized.RandReducible.of_polyTimeReducible_left}
\label{Randomized.RandReducible.of_polyTimeReducible_left}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.PolyTimeComputable.comp, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable.output_length_le, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable.pairEncode, Complexity.pairFstD, Complexity.pairSndD, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_pairFstD, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_pairSndD, Randomized.polyLen, Randomized.polyTimeComputable_sliceTake, Randomized.randProb_congr, Randomized.randProb_take, Randomized.sliceTake, Turing.pairEncode}
\difficulty{5}
Let $A$, $B$, and $C$ be languages of bit strings. If $A$ is polynomial-time reducible
to $B$ and $B$ is randomized reducible to $C$, then $A$ is randomized reducible to $C$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Composition of maps]
\lean{Randomized.composeMap}
\label{Randomized.composeMap}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.pairSndD, Randomized.sliceDrop, Randomized.sliceTake, Turing.pairEncode}
Let $f$ map Boolean lists to Boolean lists, and let $z$ be a Boolean list. For natural
numbers $a_1,k_1,a_2,k_2$, first take from $z$ the slice specified by $a_1,k_1$ and
apply $f$ to it; pair the result with the second component obtained from the
complementary slice of $z$, encode that pair, and take the slice specified by $a_2,k_2$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Composition on encoded pairs]
\lean{Randomized.composeMap_pairEncode}
\label{Randomized.composeMap_pairEncode}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.composeMap, Randomized.polyLen, Randomized.sliceDrop, Randomized.sliceTake, Turing.pairEncode}
\difficulty{1}
Let $a_1,k_1,a_2,k_2$ be natural numbers, let $f$ map Boolean strings to Boolean
strings, and let $x,t$ be Boolean strings. Applying the composition map to the encoding
of $(x,t)$ gives the encoding whose first component is $f$ applied to the encoding of
$x$ together with the first $a_1(|x|+1)^{k_1}$ bits of $t$, and whose second component
is the first $a_2(|y|+1)^{k_2}$ bits of the remaining suffix of $t$, where $y$ is that
first component.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Polynomial-Time Closure Under Composition Map]
\lean{Randomized.polyTimeComputable_composeMap}
\label{Randomized.polyTimeComputable_composeMap}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.PolyTimeComputable, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable.comp, Complexity.PolyTimeComputable.pairEncode, Complexity.polyTimeComputable_pairSndD, Randomized.composeMap, Randomized.polyTimeComputable_sliceDrop, Randomized.polyTimeComputable_sliceTake}
\difficulty{1}
Let $a_1,k_1,a_2,k_2\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $f$ be a polynomial-time computable function
on bit strings. For a bit string $z$ that decodes as a pair $(u,v)$, form $z_1=\langle
u, v_{\le L_1}\rangle$, where $L_1=a_1(|u|+1)^{k_1}$ and $v_{\le L_1}$ is the prefix of
$v$ of length at most $L_1$. Decode the remaining suffix after that prefix as the second
component of a pair, apply $f$ to $z_1$, pair its output with that suffix, and truncate
the resulting second component to length $L_2=a_2(|f(z_1)|+1)^{k_2}$. The function on
bit strings defined by this procedure, using empty strings for failed pair decodings, is
polynomial-time computable.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Polynomial Length Bound Under Pair Encoding]
\lean{Randomized.polyLen_length_pairEncode_le}
\label{Randomized.polyLen_length_pairEncode_le}
\leanok
\uses{Randomized.polyLen, Turing.length_pairEncode, Turing.pairEncode}
\difficulty{4}
Let $f$ map bit strings to bit strings, and suppose there are $C,c\in\mathbb{N}$ such
that $|f(z)|\le C(|z|+1)^c$ for every bit string $z$. For $a_1,k_1,a_2,k_2\in\mathbb{N}$
and bit strings $x,r$ with $|r|=a_1(|x|+1)^{k_1}$, the polynomial length bound with
parameters $a_2,k_2$ applied to the length of $f(\langle x,r\rangle)$ is at most the
bound with coefficient $a_2((C+1)(a_1+3)^c)^{k_2}$ and exponent $(k_1+1)ck_2$ applied to
$|x|$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Closure under randomized reductions]
\lean{Randomized.InBPP.of_randReducible}
\label{Randomized.InBPP.of_randReducible}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.PolyTimeComputable.output_length_le, Complexity.preimage_mem_P, Randomized.InBPP, Randomized.InBPP.inBPPAt_23_24, Randomized.InBPPAt.inBPP_of_5_8, Randomized.boolVerifier, Randomized.composeMap, Randomized.composeMap_pairEncode, Randomized.polyLen, Randomized.polyLen_length_pairEncode_le, Randomized.polyTimeComputable_composeMap, Randomized.polyTimeModel, Randomized.polyTimeModel_closedUnderMajority, Randomized.randProb, Randomized.randProb_append_ge, Randomized.randProb_congr, Randomized.randProb_take, Turing.pairEncode}
\difficulty{6}
Let $B$ and $C$ be languages of bit strings. If $B$ is randomized reducible to $C$ and
$C$ belongs to the bounded-error class defined by the specified polynomial-time verifier
model, then $B$ belongs to that class as well.
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}[Randomized reductions to three-clause satisfiability]
\lean{Randomized.BPNP}
\statementsource{arora-barak-ch07-randomized-computation}{pdf-26d95080dbde-p015-b002}
\label{Randomized.BPNP}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.SAT3}
$\mathrm{BPNP}$ is the set of Boolean languages that are randomized reducible to the
language of satisfiable 3-CNF formulas.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[NP Containment in BPNP]
\lean{Randomized.NP_subset_BPNP}
\label{Randomized.NP_subset_BPNP}
\leanok
\uses{Complexity.NP, Complexity.SAT3_NPHard, Randomized.BPNP, Randomized.RandReducible.of_polyTimeReducible}
\difficulty{1}
Fix a verifier model $E$. Every language in $\mathrm{NP}$ belongs to $\mathrm{BPNP}$,
the class of languages that reduce to $3$-CNF satisfiability in the randomized reduction
relation determined by $E$.
\end{theorem}
